```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
```

This vignette shows how to build the three standard graphical summaries of
decision uncertainty from a probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA): the
cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC), the cost-effectiveness
acceptability frontier (CEAF), and the expected loss curves (ELCs). It
follows the definitions in Alarid-Escudero et al. (2019) and uses the
bundled Sick-Sicker model.

## Three Questions, Three Curves

All three curves are computed from the same PSA output: the net monetary
benefit of strategy $d$ in iteration $i$ at a willingness-to-pay (WTP)
threshold $\lambda$,

$$B_{i,d}(\lambda) = \lambda E_{i,d} - C_{i,d}$$

They differ in the question they answer:

| Curve | Question | Function |
|:------|:---------|:---------|
| **CEAC** | How likely is each strategy to be the best? | `compute_ceac()` |
| **CEAF** | How likely is the *optimal* strategy to be the best? | `compute_ceaf()` |
| **ELC** | How much do I expect to lose by choosing each strategy? | `compute_expected_loss()` |

## Setup

```{r load}
library(ShinyCEA)
m <- cea_sick_sicker()
strategies <- m$info()$strategies
set.seed(20250605)
psa <- run_psa(m, m$default_params(), n_sim = 1000)
cat("Iterations used:", psa$used, "| Dropped:", psa$dropped)
```

## Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (CEAC)

The probability that strategy $d$ is cost-effective is the share of PSA
iterations in which it has the highest net benefit (Fenwick et al., 2001):

$$\Pr(\text{CE})_d(\lambda) = \frac{N_d(\lambda)}{N}$$

where $N_d$ is the number of iterations in which $d$ is the best strategy
and $N$ is the number of iterations.

```{r ceac}
ceac <- compute_ceac(psa$results, strategies,
                     wtp_max = 200000, wtp_step = 5000)
head(ceac)
plot_ceac(ceac)
```

At every WTP the probabilities add up to one across strategies:

```{r ceac-check}
tapply(ceac$ProbCE, ceac$WTP, sum)[1:5]
```

## Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Frontier (CEAF)

A risk-neutral decision-maker chooses the strategy with the highest
*expected* net benefit, whatever its probability of being cost-effective.
The CEAF follows that optimal strategy across WTP thresholds (Barton et al.,
2008):

$$d^*(\lambda) = \arg\max_d \; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} B_{i,d}(\lambda)$$

and plots $\Pr(\text{CE})_{d^*}(\lambda)$.

```{r ceaf}
ceaf <- compute_ceaf(psa$results, strategies,
                     wtp_max = 200000, wtp_step = 5000)
head(ceaf)
```

Each row gives the optimal strategy at that WTP, its probability of being
cost-effective, and its expected NMB. The WTP values at which the optimal
strategy switches are:

```{r ceaf-switch}
switches <- which(ceaf$Strategy[-1] != ceaf$Strategy[-nrow(ceaf)]) + 1
ceaf[switches, c("WTP", "Strategy", "ProbCE")]
```

Pass the frontier to `plot_ceac()` to superimpose it on the CEAC. Compute
both on the same WTP grid so the markers sit on the curves:

```{r ceac-ceaf}
plot_ceac(ceac, ceaf = ceaf)
```

**Interpretation:** The squares mark the optimal strategy at each WTP. Where
the squares sit on the highest curve, the optimal strategy is also the one
most likely to be cost-effective. Where they sit on a lower curve, the two
disagree --- this happens when the distribution of net benefit is skewed, so
a strategy can win in most iterations yet have a lower mean. The check below
counts the WTP values where this occurs:

```{r ceaf-vs-ceac}
top_ceac <- tapply(ceac$ProbCE, ceac$WTP, max)
sum(ceaf$ProbCE < top_ceac[as.character(ceaf$WTP)] - 1e-12)
```

A count of zero means that, for this model, the optimal strategy is also the
most probable one at every threshold. That is a property of this PSA, not of
the method: always check rather than reading the optimal strategy off the
highest CEAC.

## Expected Loss Curves (ELCs)

The CEAC and the CEAF report how *often* a strategy is the wrong choice, not
how much is lost when it is. The expected loss of strategy $d$ is the average
net benefit forgone by choosing it instead of the best strategy in each
iteration (Eckermann et al., 2008; Alarid-Escudero et al., 2019):

$$L_{i,d}(\lambda) = \max_{d'} B_{i,d'}(\lambda) - B_{i,d}(\lambda), \qquad
\text{EL}_d(\lambda) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} L_{i,d}(\lambda)$$

```{r el}
el <- compute_expected_loss(psa$results, strategies,
                            wtp_max = 200000, wtp_step = 5000)
head(el)
```

Set `show_optimal = TRUE` to mark the lower envelope of the curves:

```{r el-plot}
plot_expected_loss(el, show_optimal = TRUE)
```

**Interpretation:** The lowest curve at a given WTP is the optimal strategy,
so the ELC conveys the same decision as the CEAF. The vertical gap between
two curves is how much worse one strategy is than the other in expected
dollars, which also ranks the non-optimal strategies --- useful when the
optimal one cannot be implemented.

When the curves are close together, a log scale on the y-axis magnifies the
differences. Zero losses cannot be drawn on a log axis and are dropped:

```{r el-log}
plot_expected_loss(el, show_optimal = TRUE, log_scale = TRUE)
```

## How the Three Curves Connect

The expected loss of the optimal strategy equals the EVPI, and the strategy
with the lowest expected loss is the CEAF strategy. Both identities can be
verified directly:

```{r identities}
evpi <- compute_evpi(psa$results, strategies,
                     wtp_max = 200000, wtp_step = 5000)

# Lowest expected loss and the strategy that attains it, per WTP
min_el <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(el, el$WTP), function(d) {
  d[which.min(d$Expected_Loss), ]
}))

all.equal(min_el$Expected_Loss, evpi$EVPI, tolerance = 1e-6)
identical(min_el$Strategy, ceaf$Strategy)
```

A side-by-side table at selected thresholds, in the layout of Table 1 of
Alarid-Escudero et al. (2019):

```{r table}
wtp_show <- c(50000, 100000, 150000)
tab <- merge(ceac[ceac$WTP %in% wtp_show, ],
             el[el$WTP %in% wtp_show, ],
             by = c("WTP", "Strategy"))
tab$ProbCE <- round(tab$ProbCE, 2)
tab$Expected_Loss <- round(tab$Expected_Loss)
tab$Optimal <- ifelse(
  tab$Strategy == ceaf$Strategy[match(tab$WTP, ceaf$WTP)], "*", "")
tab[order(tab$WTP, tab$Expected_Loss), ]
```

Reading the two columns together shows what the CEAC alone hides. The
strategies at the bottom of each block have nearly the same probability of
being cost-effective (close to zero), yet their expected losses differ by
thousands of dollars, so the CEAC cannot rank them while the ELC can. The
reverse also occurs in practice: strategies with very different
probabilities but almost identical expected losses (Alarid-Escudero et al.,
2019, Table 1).

## Choosing What to Report

| | CEAC | CEAF | ELC |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Probability each strategy is cost-effective | Yes | Optimal only | No |
| Identifies the optimal strategy | No | Yes | Yes |
| Magnitude of a wrong decision | No | No | Yes |
| Ranking of all strategies | No | No | Yes |
| Value of further research (EVPI) | No | No | Yes |

Alarid-Escudero et al. (2019) recommend reporting ELCs as a complement to
the CEAC, the CEAF, and the EVPI rather than as a replacement. One
limitation to keep in mind: expected loss is an average, so a few very large
losses can be hidden by many small ones.

## In the Shiny App

The **CEAC** tab of `run_cea_app()` shows the same outputs: tick
*Superimpose the acceptability frontier (CEAF)* to overlay the frontier on
the CEAC, and the expected loss curves are drawn below it.

## References

- Alarid-Escudero, F., Enns, E. A., Kuntz, K. M., Michaud, T. L., & Jalal, H.
  (2019). "Time Traveling Is Just Too Dangerous" but some methods are worth
  revisiting: The advantages of expected loss curves over cost-effectiveness
  acceptability curves and frontier. *Value in Health*, 22(5), 611-618.
- Barton, G. R., Briggs, A. H., & Fenwick, E. A. L. (2008). Optimal
  cost-effectiveness decisions: The role of the cost-effectiveness
  acceptability curve (CEAC), the cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier
  (CEAF), and the expected value of perfection information (EVPI).
  *Value in Health*, 11(5), 886-897.
- Eckermann, S., Briggs, A., & Willan, A. R. (2008). Health technology
  assessment in the cost-disutility plane. *Medical Decision Making*, 28(2),
  172-181.
- Fenwick, E., Claxton, K., & Sculpher, M. (2001). Representing uncertainty:
  The role of cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. *Health Economics*,
  10(8), 779-787.
